title: For the first time, astronomers have watched gas bubbling on another star’s surface

cover.alt: A fuzzy golden disc, the red giant star R Doradus imaged by the ALMA telescope, with the date 2023-07-05 below it.
cover.credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO)/W. Vlemmings et al. · CC BY 4.0

body: Stars carry the energy from their cores up to the surface in huge, hot bubbles of gas that rise, cool and sink again, like a lava lamp. This churning, called convection, gives the Sun’s surface its grainy look, but on other stars it is normally far too small to see. R Doradus is different: it is a red giant about 180 light-years away and roughly 350 times wider than the Sun. In July and August 2023 the ALMA telescope array imaged it again and again, and the pictures show bubbles **75 times the size of the Sun** rising and sinking back into the star.

slides.alt: A fuzzy golden disc with dates below it running from 2023-07-05 to 2023-08-02; bright blobs on its surface shift, appear and fade from one image to the next.
slides.caption: Real ALMA images of the red giant R Doradus taken between 5 July and 2 August 2023, blended one into the next: bright bubbles of hot gas rise and sink across its surface.
slides.credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO)/W. Vlemmings et al. · CC BY 4.0 · excerpt

slides.heading: How wide, measured in Suns
slides.note: Rough figures from ESO; other estimates put R Doradus nearer 300 Suns wide

slides.text: This is the first time the bubbling surface of a real star can be shown in such a way.
slides.attribution: Wouter Vlemmings, Chalmers University of Technology, who led the study

left.label: Our Sun
left.text: Its surface is covered in small grains of rising hot gas, a pattern that is hard to see on distant stars.

right.label: R Doradus
right.text: Each bubble is about 75 times the size of the whole Sun, and the pattern changes on a cycle of about a month.

slides.prompt: R Doradus has roughly the same mass as the Sun. Why does that make it interesting?
slides.answer: It is a preview of our Sun’s future
slides.detail: In about five billion years the Sun should swell into a red giant and look fairly similar to R Doradus.

slides.question: What surprised astronomers about the bubbles on R Doradus?
slides.explanation: The bubbles seem to come and go on a one-month cycle, faster than expected from how convection works on the Sun. Nobody yet knows why.

source.label: ESO: Astronomers track bubbles on star’s surface in most detailed video yet
